sections.overview: The Murray cod is a large freshwater predator endemic to eastern Australia. Unlike true cod, it belongs to Percichthyidae, alongside the related trout cod and eastern freshwater cod. It is Australia’s largest freshwater fish.
sections.identification: Its robust, elongated body carries a broad, flattened head, small eyes and a wide mouth with fine teeth; the snout profile is concave. Adults commonly measure under 70 cm, while exceptional historical fish reached about 1.8 m and 113.5 kg. Olive-green flanks bear darker marbling and fade to a pale belly. Rounded fins frame a long dorsal fin with a notch between spiny and soft parts. The mouth reaches behind the eyes; the lower jaw may protrude. Maximum lifespan estimates range from 75 to 114 years.
sections.habitat: Deep pools, boulders, undercut banks and submerged fallen timber provide ambush cover and shelter. The fish is most characteristic of lowland rivers, though it also occurs in some upland reaches. Its native range spans the Murray–Darling Basin in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia, excluding the coldest upper reaches.
sections.diet: Adults take crayfish, freshwater shrimp and fish, including introduced carp and redfin when available; molluscs and occasionally small animals from the water’s edge broaden the menu. It hunts by ambush from cover.
sections.behavior: Territorial, it favors deep pools beside logs, boulders or overhanging banks. By day it shelters; at night it may hunt shallows or the surface.
sections.reproduction: Maturity usually comes at about five years, though growth and location alter the timing. In spring, pairs court and choose hard surfaces, often submerged logs or rocks. The female lays eggs on this submerged surface; the male fertilises them externally. The male guards and fans the eggs until free-swimming larvae hatch. The larvae drift away, use their yolk reserves, then feed on tiny invertebrates as they develop.
sections.ecology: A top predator, it eats native fish, crustaceans and introduced carp in the same river food webs.
sections.conservation: Overfishing sharply reduced stocks from the nineteenth century; dams, altered flows, cold releases and snag removal still damage habitat and recruitment. The species is listed as Vulnerable under Australia’s EPBC Act; this national conservation status is distinct from local fishing regulations.
